title: native backend: process aborts when two async tasks write @stdio concurrently
body:
Two concurrent connection handlers writing `@stdio.stdout` abort the
whole process on the native backend. Found in a CalDAV server project
where every request writes an access-log line: the first pair of
parallel client connections kills the server.

### Environment
- moonbitlang/async 0.22.5 (pinned), moonc v0.10.20
- macOS 26 arm64, native release build

### Minimal reproduction (20 lines, no other project code)

```moonbit
async fn main {
  let server = @socket.TcpServer(@socket.Addr::parse("127.0.0.1:18096"), reuse_addr=true)
  server.run_forever((conn, _) => {
    let buf = FixedArray::make(1024, b'\x00')
    let _ = conn.read(buf, max_len=1024)
    @stdio.stdout.write("handled a connection\n")
    conn.write("HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nhi")
    conn.close()
  })
}
```

Two clients connect simultaneously:

```
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as ex:  # both connect at once
    ...both send GET, both receive responses...
```

### Observed

- Both clients receive their responses, then the whole process dies with
  no output at all (native abort; no panic message on stderr).
- Control: the same burst against a variant that does NOT write
  @stdio.stdout survives — the trigger is the concurrent @stdio write.
- A single connection never crashes; it takes two handlers interleaving
  at the write.

### Expected

Concurrent @stdio writes from two spawned connection tasks should
interleave (or be serialized by the runtime) instead of aborting the
process.

### Workaround in the application

A global `@async.Semaphore(1)` around every @stdio write
(release after) makes the same burst fully stable — suggesting the fix
belongs in the runtime's stdio layer rather than the application.

### Notes
- Reproduces on the release build; 10-connection bursts also abort
  (5/10 connections handled before the abort).
- `@async.Semaphore` is documented as an async-primitive counter, so the
  serialization workaround behaves correctly under load.

title: [http] @http.post ignores Content-Length and sends non-empty bodies as chunked
body:
## Summary

`@http.post(url, body, headers~)` ignores an explicit `Content-Length` in
`headers~`. For every non-empty body tested, the request is sent with
`Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and no `Content-Length` header.

The body itself is transmitted. A chunked-aware server receives the complete
payload and returns 200. The interoperability problem occurs with servers or
proxies that require a known-length request and do not decode chunked request
bodies; those endpoints observe an empty body or fail while parsing it.

## Environment

- Reproduced with `moonbitlang/async` 0.22.9, the current registry release.
- Native and wasm/moonrun produce the same wire headers.
- String and Bytes bodies produce the same behavior.
- Toolchain: `moon 0.1.20261104`.

## Reproduction

```moonbit
----
import {
  "moonbitlang/async@0.22.9",
  "moonbitlang/async@0.22.9/http",
  "moonbitlang/core/encoding/utf8",
}
----

async fn main {
  let headers : Map[@http.CaseInsensitiveString, String] = Map([])
  headers[@http.CaseInsensitiveString("Content-Type")] = "application/json"
  let payload = @utf8.encode("{\"x\":1}")
  headers[@http.CaseInsensitiveString("Content-Length")] =
    payload.length().to_string()

  let (response, body) = @http.post(
    "http://127.0.0.1:8080/echo",
    payload,
    headers=headers,
  )
  println("status=\{response.code} body=\{body.text()}")
}
```

Observed request headers:

```text
Content-Length: <absent>
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
```

The server decoded the complete body, confirming that the payload was sent and
that the issue is request framing/header selection.

## Cause

`src/http/request.mbt:107` passes `headers~` to `Client::connect`; line 109
calls `Client::request` without per-request `extra_headers`.
`src/http/send.mbt:37-39` includes `Content-Length` in `forbidden_headers`,
and `Sender::new` drops it at lines 67-80. As a result,
`send_request` enters `WaitingRequestBody` and emits chunked encoding
(`src/http/send.mbt:348-353`).

## Suggested fix

For a body with known length, send an explicit `Content-Length` and use a
fixed-length entity. If connection-wide headers and per-request headers need
different treatment, keep them separate and pass request headers through
`Client::request(..., extra_headers)`.

Please add a regression test that verifies the server receives
`Content-Length` equal to the payload length for `@http.post`.

title: [http] TCP reset aborts the entire HTTP server process
body:
## Summary

A TCP reset while an HTTP/WebSocket connection has an active read pipeline
can terminate the entire `@http.Server::run_forever` process. The failure is
an uncatchable `guard!` assertion, not a typed error, so handler-level error
handling cannot isolate the affected connection.

The failure path is:

1. `ServerConnection::read_request` calls `Reader::skip_body`.
2. The reset causes `skip_body` to exit without changing `self.body` from a
   non-empty state to `Empty`.
3. `Reader::read_request` evaluates `guard! self.body is Empty`.
4. `guard!` aborts the process.

## Environment

- Reproduced with `moonbitlang/async` 0.22.9, the current registry release.
- 0.22.9, native: 3/3 runs terminated with exit code 134.
- 0.22.7, wasm/moonrun: 3/3 runs terminated with the same failure.
- Toolchain: `moon 0.1.20261104`.
- `parser.mbt` and `server.mbt` at upstream `main` `c9ec9df` are
  byte-identical to `v0.22.9`.

The corresponding checks are at `src/http/parser.mbt:373`
(`read_request`), `src/http/parser.mbt:428` (`read_response`), and
`src/http/parser.mbt:459-466` (`skip_body`).

## Reproduction

Start a server using `@http.Server::run_forever` with a WebSocket-upgrade
handler. Then run:

```python
import base64
import os
import socket
import struct
import time


def upgrade(sock):
    key = base64.b64encode(os.urandom(16)).decode()
    request = (
        "GET /ws HTTP/1.1\r\n"
        "Host: localhost\r\n"
        "Upgrade: websocket\r\n"
        "Connection: Upgrade\r\n"
        f"Sec-WebSocket-Key: {key}\r\n"
        "Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n"
        "\r\n"
    )
    sock.sendall(request.encode())
    sock.settimeout(2)
    try:
        sock.recv(1024)
        return True
    except OSError:
        return False


sockets = []
for _ in range(50):
    sock = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 7301))
    if upgrade(sock):
        sockets.append(sock)

for sock in sockets:
    sock.setsockopt(
        socket.SOL_SOCKET,
        socket.SO_LINGER,
        struct.pack("ii", 1, 0),
    )
    sock.close()

time.sleep(1.5)
print(f"RST-closed {len(sockets)} upgraded connections")
```

The server exits with code 134 in every run above. Non-WebSocket variants
tested during the investigation, including partial POST bodies with RST,
truncated headers with RST/FIN, and serial FIN closes, did not trigger the
failure.

## Observed stack

```text
PanicError
    at Reader::read_request
    at ServerConnection::read_request
    at Reader::skip_body
    at impl Reader with drop
```

Release builds terminate without diagnostics and report only exit code 134.

## Impact

This was the only robustness failure observed in an 800,000-connection
WebSocket campaign. The 800,000-connection run remained stable until graceful
shutdown; connection teardown is the exposed failure mode.

## Suggested fix

At minimum, set `self.body = Empty` when `skip_body` reaches EOF or a short
read. The next transport read can then raise `@io.ReaderClosed` and close only
that connection.

Alternatively, replace the `guard!` with a typed error such as
`@io.ReaderClosed`, allowing `run_forever`'s per-connection failure handling
to contain the failure.

Please add a regression test that upgrades a connection, resets it while the
read pipeline is active, and verifies that the server remains alive.

title: A public way to run an async function to completion from synchronous code
body:
We are writing a WSGI-style adapter: a synchronous host calls an async application once per request and needs its result before returning.

The only entry today is `run_async_main`. It is doc-hidden, missing on wasm-gc (#389 may change that), returns before the coroutine finishes on js, and exits the process when the coroutine raises, so the error never reaches the caller. Nothing tells the caller whether it is already inside the loop either.

Would you accept two public functions?

```moonbit
pub fn in_loop() -> Bool

pub fn block_on(main : async () -> Unit raise) -> Unit raise
```

`block_on` runs `main` to completion on the calling thread and hands its error back. It refuses when the caller is already inside the loop, and on a target that cannot block (js).

If the `EventLoop` API discussed in #526 lands, `block_on` could be a thin layer over `handle_events`. We are happy to wait for that, or to send a PR in whichever shape you prefer.

title: `@fs.Watcher` panics on Linux when a new watch's events arrive before the watch is in `InotifyWatcher::watched`
body:
On Linux, a program that waits on `@fs.Watcher` aborts with a panic when files are created and written in the watched tree. It happens within a second or two under steady file churn, and now and then under lighter churn, such as a Kubernetes ConfigMap update.

Seen with moonbitlang/async 0.22.9 and 0.22.4, moonc v0.10.20 and v0.10.17, native target, Linux aarch64. `main` (d899d8a6) has the same code.

### Reproduction

`main/main.mbt` (the package imports `moonbitlang/async`, `moonbitlang/async/fs` and `moonbitlang/core/env`):

```moonbit
async fn main {
  let dir = @env.args()[1]
  let watcher = @fs.Watcher(dir)
  defer watcher.close()
  let mut changes = 0
  for ;; {
    watcher.wait_any()
    changes += 1
    println("changes: \{changes}")
  }
}
```

`churn.py`, four writers that each create a file, write it for 50 ms, create, write and remove a second file, then remove the first:

```python
import os, sys, time, threading
d = sys.argv[1]; secs = float(sys.argv[2])
end = time.time() + secs
def worker(k):
    i = 0
    while time.time() < end:
        p = os.path.join(d, f"w{k}-{i%20}.db")
        with open(p, "w") as f:
            t = time.time() + 0.05
            while time.time() < t:
                f.write("x" * 512); f.flush()
        j = p + "-journal"
        with open(j, "w") as f:
            for _ in range(50):
                f.write("j" * 512); f.flush()
        os.remove(j)
        os.remove(p)
        i += 1
ts = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(k,)) for k in range(4)]
[t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
```

```sh
mkdir watched
moon build --target native --release
./_build/native/release/build/main/main.exe watched &
python3 churn.py watched 30
```

The program aborts (SIGABRT, exit status 134) after 1.0 to 1.5 s in each of three runs. The stack of a debug build's core, from gdb:

```
#3 moonbit_panic
#4 Map::at[Int, moonbitlang/async/internal/event_loop.FileIdentity]
#5 moonbitlang/async/fs InotifyWatcher::process_events
#6 moonbitlang/async/fs InotifyWatcher::process_events (closure)
#7 moonbitlang/async/internal/event_loop IoHandle::wait_read
```

### Cause

`InotifyWatcher::process_events` looks up the watch of each relevant event with `self.watched[wd]`, which panics when `wd` is not in the map. `InotifyWatcher::add_file` puts a new watch in the map only after `@event_loop.inotify_add_watch` has run in a worker thread and the calling task has resumed. The kernel delivers events for the new watch at once, so `process_events` can read one before the map has it. This happens when `Watcher::get_file_at` adds a file or directory that is being written.

`Watcher::mark_as_modified` could panic the same way, at `self.watched[id]`. `Watcher::wait_aux` removes a file's identity from `watched` before it calls `remove_file`, and the watch can deliver events until its `IN_IGNORED` is read. The reproduction did not hit this one.

### A possible fix

With this change applied to a local copy of 0.22.9, the program ran through three 30 s runs of `churn.py`. Before the churn it reported each change, one by one: a file created, an append to it, a new subdirectory, a file in it and an append to that file. After the churn, it reported a single append too.

```diff
--- a/src/fs/watch_inotify.mbt
+++ b/src/fs/watch_inotify.mbt
@@ -303,8 +303,14 @@
       }
 
       if buf.has_relevant_event(offset) {
-        let id = self.watched[wd]
-        self.watcher.mark_as_modified(id)
+        match self.watched.get(wd) {
+          Some(id) => self.watcher.mark_as_modified(id)
+          // `add_file` puts a new watch in `watched` once
+          // `inotify_add_watch` has returned, and the watch's first events
+          // can come before that: look at the whole tree again, as after
+          // an overflow, so that no change is lost.
+          None => self.watcher.overflow()
+        }
       }
     }
   }
--- a/src/fs/watch.mbt
+++ b/src/fs/watch.mbt
@@ -775,7 +775,9 @@
 
 ///|
 fn Watcher::mark_as_modified(self : Watcher, id : FileIdentity) -> Unit {
-  let file = self.watched[id]
+  // A file removed from the tree may still get events until its watch's
+  // `IN_IGNORED` comes.
+  guard self.watched.get(id) is Some(file) else { return }
   if file.modified {
     return
   }
```

Ignoring an event whose watch is not known would also stop the panic. It can lose a write made in that window, though. Treating it like an overflow rescans the tree, and the window is short, so it should be rare.

title: Avoid 1 KiB writes for large fixed-length HTTP responses
body:
In `moonbitlang/async@0.22.7` and current `main`, the HTTP sender allocates a private 1 KiB buffer per connection. The `SendingFixed` path copies each body slice through that buffer and flushes it repeatedly. `ServerConnection::write_reader` uses the same buffer in this mode. The public `Server` and `ServerConnection` constructors offer no way to size it.

This affects static file servers such as [`cli/serve`](https://github.com/moonbit-community/cmd/blob/4190db7/commands/serve/files.mbt), which read files in 64 KiB blocks and send responses with an explicit `Content-Length`.

A minimal response body that exercises the path:

```moonbit
conn.send_response(200, "OK", extra_headers={ "Content-Length": "67108864" })
let block = Bytes::make(65536, b'x')
for _ in 0..<1024 {
  conn.write(block)
}
conn.end_response()
```

From the [sender implementation](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/v0.22.7/src/http/send.mbt), 64 MiB of body data requires about 65,536 writes to the underlying writer, plus header overhead. Passing the original blocks through would need about 1,024 writes when the underlying writer accepts each block in full. These are source-derived call counts.

Could the fixed-length path flush pending bytes and pass large slices directly to the underlying writer? It should preserve wire ordering, account for partial writes, and keep the `Content-Length` checks. A public send-buffer size would also let callers tune the buffered path.

title: `@socket.UdpServer`: a `reuse_port_lb` option, as `TcpServer` has
body:
`TcpServer` takes `reuse_port_lb` (#525): on Linux it sets `SO_REUSEPORT` before `bind`, and the kernel spreads connections across the processes bound to the port. `UdpServer` has no counterpart, and since it creates and binds the socket in one call, a caller cannot set the option either: `UdpServer::fd` comes after `bind`.

The use case is a QUIC (HTTP/3) server with several worker processes on one port, the way the TCP side already works. With the option each worker binds the UDP port itself, and the kernel's 4-tuple hash keeps a connection's datagrams on one worker. Without it, one process has to hold the port and pass every datagram to the workers. That is what mooncat does today, at the cost of an extra hop and copy per datagram.

Proposal: `UdpServer::UdpServer(addr, dual_stack~, reuse_port_lb~ : Bool = false)`, with the same semantics and documentation as the TCP option. It takes effect on Linux only and is not set elsewhere, which keeps out the unicast pitfalls discussed in #348 (macOS and BSD hand unicast datagrams to the last socket bound; Windows has its own rules).

Happy to send a PR mirroring #525; `allow_reuse_port` in `socket.c` already does the work.

title: Expose the received cancellation signal for child-process forwarding
body:
## Problem

Please expose the signal that caused global cancellation through a supported public API. A child-process launcher needs to forward the original SIGINT or SIGTERM while it performs protected cleanup.

With published `moonbitlang/async@0.22.5`, a stock Moonrun parent receiving SIGINT exits with shell-equivalent status 130, but a child using `@process.graceful_cancel(..., signal=SIGTERM)` receives SIGTERM and reports 143. Configuring SIGINT instead reverses the problem for a parent receiving SIGTERM. The public cancellation handler cannot select between them from the cancellation request alone.

This matters for a Moonx launcher whose separate Node child owns the application's hosted services and shutdown report. The parent and child should agree on Interrupt/130 versus Terminate/143 after finalization.

## Minimal public-API reproduction

Save as `repro.mbtx`:

```moonbit
----
import {
  "moonbitlang/async@0.22.5",
  "moonbitlang/async@0.22.5/process",
  "moonbitlang/async@0.22.5/signal",
  "moonbitlang/async@0.22.5/stdio",
  "moonbitlang/core/env",
}
----

async fn main {
  let args = @env.args()
  @signal.set_global_cancellation_signals([SIGINT, SIGTERM])
  defer @async.protect_from_cancel(() => @stdio.stderr.write("PARENT_FINALIZER\n"))
  let result = @async.handle_cancellation(() => @process.run(
    args[1], args[2:].to_owned(),
    stdin=@stdio.stdin, stdout=@stdio.stdout, stderr=@stdio.stderr,
    cancel_handler=@process.graceful_cancel(timeout=200, signal=SIGTERM),
  ))
  if result is None {
    @stdio.stderr.write("PARENT_CANCELLED\n")
  }
}
```

Run it with a child that reports which signal it receives:

```sh
moonx repro.mbtx node -e '
process.on("SIGINT", () => process.stderr.write("CHILD SIGINT 130\n", () => process.exit(130)));
process.on("SIGTERM", () => process.stderr.write("CHILD SIGTERM 143\n", () => process.exit(143)));
console.log("READY " + process.pid);
setInterval(() => {}, 1000);
'
```

After the child's READY handshake, send SIGINT to only the launcher PID from another terminal. It reports CHILD SIGTERM 143 while the parent terminates as 130. Repeat with SIGTERM to the launcher: both select 143 with this fixed configuration.

The maintained downstream probes build the parent and a genuine Node-hosted Moon-Lander application separately, hold stdin open, signal only the parent, and verify actual child completion, finalization and reaping. The mismatch is reproduced with stock `0.10.16+b1a0e846e` and `0.10.17+d971670cd` on macOS arm64. Toolchain selection explicitly sets MOON_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT, MOON_HOME and PATH together. No compiler, Moonrun or canonical async source override is used.

## Requested capability

One possible additive API is a typed, non-suspending `signal.received_cancellation_signal() -> Signal?`, callable from the process cancellation handler and protected cleanup. The API name and shape are for maintainers to choose.

Useful semantics would be:

- Record the triggering signal before propagating global cancellation.
- Retain the observation through protected cleanup without consuming it or raising cancellation.
- Return no signal for ordinary task cancellation.
- Define repeated-signal precedence, ideally retaining the first signal that selected cancellation.
- Preserve current default cancellation behavior and final process status.

An equivalent public forwarding policy would also solve the use case. This does not require exposing scheduler queues, private task state or the event loop itself.

The implementation already retains `killed_by_signal` internally, including at [current source 5ec5c056](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/5ec5c05674ac134c8ed8867b4d4b2e3e9cea044c/src/internal/event_loop/event_loop.mbt). That source observation is separate from the runtime reproduction against published 0.22.5.

Related downstream tracking: https://github.com/moonrockz/moon-lander/issues/140. Related upstream #684 asks for non-cancelling signal subscriptions for interactive sessions; this narrower request observes the signal after global cancellation has already been selected. We would be glad to contribute an additive implementation and native/stock-Moonrun lifecycle tests.

title: DNS results leak when cancellation races with getaddrinfo completion
body:
Cancellation racing with DNS completion can leak the returned address-info list. This reproduces with the native backend as well as Wasm; the native reproduction below does not involve Moonrun.

Reproduced against async revision `65876dc7f983b78d9ccd814caff2f6a39a58a5ae`. The same cancellation handling is still present in [`network.mbt` on main](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/main/src/internal/event_loop/network.mbt).

Add `src/socket/dns_leak_test.mbt`:

```moonbit
///|
async test "DNS cancellation lifetime" {
  for i = 0; i < 50; i = i + 1 {
    ignore(@async.with_timeout_opt(1, () => {
      ignore(@socket.Addr::resolve("localhost", port=80))
    }))
  }
  @async.sleep(100)
}
```

Build the native test, then run it under a heap-leak detector. For example, using `leaks`:

```sh
moon test src/socket/dns_leak_test.mbt --target native --build-only
MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --quiet --list --atExit -- \
  ./_build/native/debug/test/moonbitlang/async/socket/socket.blackbox_test.exe \
  dns_leak_test.mbt:0-1
```

The race is timing-dependent; repeat the invocation if it does not occur immediately. The test's assertions report success, but the address-info allocations remain unfreed.

Three native runs produced:

| Run | Leaked allocations | Leaked bytes |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 72 | 2,592 |
| 2 | 112 | 4,032 |
| 3 | 120 | 4,320 |

Every reported allocation had a stack through:

```text
worker_loop
  → getaddrinfo_job_worker
  → getaddrinfo
  → si_list_to_addrinfo
  → si_item_to_addrinfo
  → calloc
```

The ownership gap appears in [`getaddrinfo`](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/65876dc7f983b78d9ccd814caff2f6a39a58a5ae/src/internal/event_loop/network.mbt#L25-L70):

1. The background coroutine completes the job and assigns `result = Ok(job.get_getaddrinfo_result())`.
2. Native's [result getter](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/65876dc7f983b78d9ccd814caff2f6a39a58a5ae/src/internal/event_loop/thread_pool.c#L1648-L1730) marks the result as fetched, so freeing the job no longer frees that list.
3. The waiting coroutine is cancelled before its caller receives the result and installs `defer ai_root.free()`.
4. The existing `catch { _ if result is Ok(_) => return result }` intends to handle this case, but cancellation uses a separate control-flow mechanism and bypasses ordinary exception handling.

The expected behavior is to retain an owner through this handoff. A focused correction wrapping the wait in `@coroutine.handle_cancellation`, returning an already-published `Ok` result on cancellation and otherwise re-raising cancellation, eliminated the leak. All three native control runs then reported **0 leaks / 0 bytes**, with the native C implementation and reproducer unchanged. The same correction also passed 20 focused runs on each of Moonrun's V8 and wee8 backends with host leak checking enabled.

Upstream's built-in `MOONBIT_ASYNC_CHECK_FD_LEAK` check only tracks file descriptors, so a successful native test run alone does not detect these heap leaks.

This was initially exposed by [Moonrun's wee8 conformance job](https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/actions/runs/41033982308/job/123990708878), which reported `async(addr_infos=6)` after the WebSocket tests. The native reproduction establishes that this ownership bug is not specific to the Wasm host implementation.

title: Process tests can fail under load due to exact timing and child-startup assumptions
body:
During the 2026-10-29 toolchain audit (`moonc v0.10.18+6c83a7f62`, macOS, native target), the full suite reported 673/677 passing while many repositories were being built concurrently. Four process tests failed:

- `spawn_in_group wait`: expected completion at tick #2, observed #3.
- `Process::wait`: expected tick 2, observed 3.
- `spawn_in_group cancel`: expected the child's termination-handler output, observed empty output.
- `do not kill orphan children on hard cancel`: expected `after sleep`, observed empty output.

After the load subsided, both the focused 10-test process suite and a complete 677-test native run passed without source changes. Strict native compilation also passes. This evidence points to timing/startup sensitivity in the tests; it does not establish a runtime correctness regression.

The first two tests divide elapsed wall-clock time into exact 250 ms ticks. Cancellation tests wait a fixed 300 ms before cancellation, which can precede child or grandchild initialization on a loaded machine. Consider readiness handshakes before cancellation and assertions about completion/order or lower bounds rather than exact scheduling ticks.

Commands used for the successful recheck:
```sh
moon test src/process/spawn_in_group_test.mbt src/process/cancel_test.mbt --target native -j 1
moon check --target native --deny-warn
moon test --target native -j 1
```

No test expectations or production code were changed during this audit.

title: [bug] `CancelSynchronousIo` discards some read data
Feature request: support signal subscriptions without cancelling the whole async task
body:
## Problem

The public interface we consume in `moonbitlang/async@0.22.5` provides global cancellation-signal configuration. Interactive applications also need to handle a signal as an event without automatically cancelling the long-lived session.

## Concrete use case

An interactive shell is waiting for input. On Ctrl-C, it should be able to:

1. Discard the current unsubmitted input.
2. Display a new prompt.
3. Preserve variables, working directory and other session state.
4. Continue accepting commands.

Once the session task has entered cancellation, ordinary error handling cannot turn it back into a usable session.

## Requested capability

Please consider a public signal-subscription mechanism through which applications can receive supported signals and decide whether to cancel a task.

The contract would need to clarify:

- Interaction with global cancellation-signal configuration.
- Behavior with multiple subscribers.
- Unsubscription and resource cleanup.
- Coexistence with handlers owned by a host application.
- Signal coalescing/loss and platform support boundaries.

## Scope

The initial use case is Ctrl-C recovery while an interactive session is idle and reading input.

Forwarding signals to foreground process groups, stopping/resuming jobs and terminal ownership require additional process-control capabilities. Signal subscriptions alone would not complete those features.

Related: #670 discusses host ownership of signal handling, and #648 covers managed process-group cleanup.

This request comes from [cmd](https://github.com/moonbit-community/cmd) and is based on the consumed 0.22.5 public interface. It does not claim a fresh runtime test of main.

## Problem

Command-line tools need to determine whether input or output is connected to a terminal and query its window size. We could not find these capabilities in the public interface of `moonbitlang/async@0.22.5` that we consume.

## Concrete use cases

- `test -t` needs terminal detection for the specified descriptor.
- jq needs terminal detection to enable automatic color appropriately.
- column needs terminal width for its default layout.
- Redirected output should avoid automatic terminal-specific presentation.

A character device is not necessarily a terminal. Environment variables also cannot reliably substitute for detecting the actual endpoint.

## Requested capability

An initial API for:

- Terminal detection on standard streams or other supported handles.
- Terminal row and column queries.

Please distinguish a non-terminal endpoint, a query failure and an unsupported backend, and document Windows console and Wasm host support.

## Scope and current workaround

This request is limited to detection and size queries. Raw mode, PTYs and foreground/background job control can be discussed separately and need not block an initial API.

In [cmd](https://github.com/moonbit-community/cmd), explicit color options, explicit width and COLUMNS are available alternatives, but do not provide automatic terminal behavior.

title: Feature request: expose readlink for reading a symbolic link's stored target
body:
## Problem

The public interface we consume in `moonbitlang/async@0.22.5` supports creating symbolic links and resolving existing paths with `realpath`, but we could not find an operation to read the target stored in a symbolic link.

## Concrete use case

A link may store:

```text
../shared/config
```

A tree utility needs to display that target, and a copy utility needs to recreate the link with its original target. Reading and copying a dangling link should remain possible even if its referent does not exist.

A resolved canonical path cannot preserve this original relative target and does not replace readlink.

## Requested capability

Please consider a public operation such as `fs.readlink(path)`, with a contract covering:

- Returning the stored target without following the final link.
- Relative, absolute and dangling targets.
- A clear error for a non-link.
- Support boundaries for Windows symbolic links, junctions and other reparse points.
- How targets that cannot be represented losslessly as ordinary strings are handled.

The name is illustrative; the final representation should follow the library's path API design.

## Current workaround and scope

In [cmd](https://github.com/moonbit-community/cmd), tree conservatively rejects links it cannot represent correctly, and related copying/path-resolution features remain limited.

Directory traversal and output formatting are downstream implementation work. This request is specifically for access to the stored link target.

The gap is based on the consumed 0.22.5 public interface, not a fresh verification of main.

title: Feature request: support setting file access and modification times
body:
## Problem

The public interface we consume in `moonbitlang/async@0.22.5` exposes access and modification time queries, but we could not find corresponding setters.

This blocks updating existing files with touch and preserving timestamps after copying, moving across filesystems or extracting files.

## Concrete use cases

- `touch existing-file` should update timestamps without changing file contents.
- `touch -a` or `touch -m` should update only the selected timestamp.
- Copying or extraction may need to restore a recorded modification time.
- A cross-filesystem move needs to restore timestamps during the copy phase before considering source deletion.

Rewriting contents does not implement these semantics.

## Requested capability

Path-based or file-handle-based setters supporting:

- An explicit timestamp.
- The current time.
- Leaving either timestamp unchanged.
- Explicit follow/no-follow semantics for path operations.
- Documented precision, platform limitations and permission errors.

This request concerns access and modification times, not directly setting ctime.

## Suggested validation

Check that existing file contents remain unchanged, that updating one timestamp preserves the other, and that symbolic-link behavior is explicit. Account for timestamp rounding by the underlying filesystem.

If a Wasm host does not support the operation, an explicit unsupported result would be preferable to silently ignoring it.

## Scope

This is a feature request from [cmd](https://github.com/moonbit-community/cmd), based on the consumed 0.22.5 public interface. It does not claim fresh execution against main.

title: Feature request: support setting file length through an open File handle
body:
## Problem

The public interface we consume in `moonbitlang/async@0.22.5` provides opening modes such as `TruncateExisting`, but we could not find an operation to set the length of an already-open `File`.

For tools that must inspect a destination before deciding whether to overwrite it, truncating at open time is too early. Checking first and then reopening by pathname can select a different object.

## Concrete use cases

An existing-file overwrite needs this sequence:

1. Open source and destination without truncating.
2. Inspect the opened objects' identities and reject same-file or hard-link aliases.
3. Truncate that same destination handle.
4. Write the new contents while retaining the destination's inode relationships.

A downloader retry has a similar need: reset the output file already opened for the first attempt without resolving its pathname again.

## Requested capability

Please consider a method such as `File::set_len` or `File::truncate`. These names are illustrative, not a proposed final signature.

The contract should specify:

- A length type suitable for large files.
- Shrinking and extension behavior.
- Errors for read-only handles, special files and invalid lengths.
- Whether the current file offset changes.
- Native and Wasm support.

The safe-copy workflow also needs file identity queries; truncation alone would not complete it.

## Current workaround and scope

In [cmd](https://github.com/moonbit-community/cmd), relevant existing-destination cases in cp, split and csplit are rejected. Downloader retry reset uses path-based reopening, with a documented concurrent-path-replacement limitation.

Temporary-file-plus-rename is useful for some replacement operations, but cannot substitute for an overwrite that must retain the existing inode.

This request is based on the public interface of the consumed 0.22.5 release, not a fresh runtime test of main.

title: Feature request: expose file identity and permission metadata
body:
## Problem

We are implementing command-line utilities in pure MoonBit in [moonbit-community/cmd](https://github.com/moonbit-community/cmd). In the public interface of `moonbitlang/async@0.22.5` that we consume, file kind, size, timestamps and access checks are available, but we could not find file identity or permission-mode queries.

This prevents callers from making some necessary decisions before modifying a file.

## Concrete use cases

- Before overwriting a destination, `cp` must detect whether source and destination are hard-link aliases of the same file. Truncating first would destroy the source.
- Default copying and `patch` writeback need the source permission mode to set the permissions of a new or replacement file correctly.
- `test -ef` needs to compare file identity.
- `tail -F` needs to distinguish continued growth of an existing file from replacement of the object at its pathname.

Canonical paths, equal contents and equal timestamps cannot substitute for file identity.

## Requested capability

Metadata queries on both paths and open file handles, initially including:

- An identity suitable for same-file comparison. An opaque comparable type would be sufficient; it need not expose Unix inode numbers on every platform.
- Permission mode, with explicit platform support.
- Explicit follow/no-follow semantics for path queries.
- Handle queries that inspect the object actually referenced by the handle without resolving its pathname again.

Owner/group and link count could follow separately. Identity and mode alone would unblock several workflows.

## Current workaround and scope

We currently reject overwrites or metadata-preserving operations that we cannot implement correctly. This is a feature request based on the consumed 0.22.5 public interface, not a claim of a newly reproduced defect or a fresh verification of main.

Related: #493 covers directory-handle-relative operations. File identity and metadata queries would complement that proposal, but querying metadata alone would not eliminate all pathname races.

Clarify process-wide SIGPIPE policy and host signal-handler ownership
body:
## Summary

Could the ownership contract for SIGPIPE handling be clarified, particularly when async runs alongside native libraries or inside a host application?

At main commit `97d7672bcb43d9cc89429e458494d2de0e8622b9` (also present in published 0.22.5), thread-pool initialization unconditionally calls `signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN)`. This replaces the process-wide disposition, including an existing custom handler. Thread-pool destruction restores the calling thread's saved signal mask, but does not restore the SIGPIPE disposition.

Sources:
- [Initialization](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/97d7672bcb43d9cc89429e458494d2de0e8622b9/src/internal/event_loop/thread_pool.c#L479-L496)
- [Destruction](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/97d7672bcb43d9cc89429e458494d2de0e8622b9/src/internal/event_loop/thread_pool.c#L562-L580)
- Original intentional change: #195, to make closed-pipe writes return EPIPE instead of terminating the process.

## Concern

Returning EPIPE is desirable. The question is whether initializing an async thread pool should implicitly take ownership of signal policy for the entire process:

- A host-installed SIGPIPE handler is replaced, including for writes unrelated to async.
- The changed disposition persists after thread-pool destruction; restoring a thread signal mask does not restore a process-wide disposition.
- Native components can accidentally depend on async having initialized first to survive a broken pipe.

We noticed this while auditing Proton's standalone clipboard package. Its POSIX writer has its own broken-pipe handling gap; that remains Proton's responsibility. Async's global policy can mask that gap after thread-pool initialization. This report does not attribute Proton's defect to async.

## Suggested discussion

If async intentionally owns process-wide signal policy as an application runtime, document that contract and its implications for native embedding and existing handlers. If coexistence with host-owned signal policy is intended, consider containing suppression to async-owned I/O or offering an explicit initialization policy.

Simply saving and unconditionally restoring the previous handler is not necessarily sufficient: other code may change the disposition while async is running. Likewise, removing SIG_IGN alone would regress the original EPIPE behavior. The desired ownership contract should guide the implementation.

Useful acceptance cases would cover an existing custom handler, ordinary broken-pipe writes returning an error, and lifecycle behavior under the selected contract.

## Evidence boundary

This is source-confirmed behavior and a design/compatibility question. I have not run a native embedding regression demonstrating a specific application failure. Searching existing SIGPIPE issues found #195, but no separate discussion of host-handler preservation or lifetime ownership.

title: [tls/windows] PFX server credential import blocks the shared async event loop
body:
## Summary

The native Windows `async Tls::server_from_pair` helper performs PFX credential initialization synchronously on the coroutine/event-loop thread. Naturally slow `PFXImportCertStore` calls can prevent unrelated ready coroutines from running until their deadlines have expired.

This was observed with **both MSVC and Clang**, using `moonbitlang/async` **0.22.4**, MoonBit **0.1.20261016 / moonc 0.10.16**, on Windows Server 2025 (10.0.26100). The direct synchronous call path is also still present in main at `97d7672bcb43d9cc89429e458494d2de0e8622b9`.

The helper is explicitly internal/testing-only; this report concerns its interaction with other async tasks during TLS-based integration tests. It does not claim that the Windows PFX API itself violates its contract.

## Call path

- [`Tls::server_from_pair`](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/97d7672bcb43d9cc89429e458494d2de0e8622b9/src/tls/schannel.mbt#L283) asynchronously reads the PFX file, then directly calls `context.init_server`.
- [`moonbitlang_async_schannel_init_server`](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/97d7672bcb43d9cc89429e458494d2de0e8622b9/src/tls/schannel.c#L215) calls `PFXImportCertStore`, certificate lookup, and `AcquireCredentialsHandle` synchronously. Credential import does not cross the blocking-job/worker boundary.

Async file reading therefore does not prevent the subsequent credential import from blocking the event loop.

## Captured natural failure

We instrumented QPC, wall time, thread CPU time, IOCP waits, and producer/consumer progress in a downstream test executable. One Clang failure recorded this sequence on the same event-loop thread:

| QPC ms | Event |
| ---: | --- |
| 576209.589 | Consumer finishes its deliberate backpressure sleep |
| 576209.625 | Consumer creates a fresh 50ms body-read deadline |
| 576209.639 | Producer observes readiness |
| 576209.679 | A sibling TLS test enters server initialization |
| 576288.014 | `PFXImportCertStore` returns, after **78.303ms** |
| 576289.775 | Server initialization returns |
| 576289.937 | The 50ms body-read timeout fires |
| 576289.962 | Producer's write returns |

The consumer's backpressure was already excluded from the new deadline. A sibling test's synchronous credential import then prevented the ready producer from progressing. The failure is an ordinary expired read deadline, not evidence that the timer fired early.

A separate MSVC trace records a **513.418ms** PFX import overlapping a 200ms body-read deadline. Certificate lookup took 0.005ms and credential acquisition took 1.641ms. Both compilers observed natural PFX imports exceeding 500ms. Thread CPU increments were often zero at Windows' coarse accounting resolution; we have **not** established the Windows-internal reason for the variable latency.

The complete timeline and selected raw traces are committed at:

- [Diagnosis and limitations](https://github.com/Milky2018/wasmoon/blob/49d7286889986271050b58b973d472a269e239ee/docs/evidence/portable-interpreter-2026-10-19/http-timing-diagnosis.md)
- [Natural 50ms backpressure failure](https://github.com/Milky2018/wasmoon/blob/49d7286889986271050b58b973d472a269e239ee/docs/evidence/portable-interpreter-2026-10-19/http-timing-natural-backpressure.log)
- [Natural MSVC 200ms deadline failure](https://github.com/Milky2018/wasmoon/blob/49d7286889986271050b58b973d472a269e239ee/docs/evidence/portable-interpreter-2026-10-19/http-timing-natural-deadline.log)

## Reproduction and controls

The downstream HTTP timing tests and the TLS trust-verification server initially shared a whitebox test executable. The generated driver runs up to ten async tests on one event loop. `moon test --no-parallelize` serializes executables but does not serialize their internal async tests.

[Windows diagnostic run 39263705985](https://github.com/Milky2018/wasmoon/actions/runs/39263705985) tested four cohorts 300 times each per compiler after a complete native workspace run:

1. Complete whitebox test executable, including TLS and HTTP timing tests.
2. The two initially failing positive HTTP tests alone.
3. Those two tests plus TLS.
4. All nine HTTP timeout tests without TLS.

Natural failures occurred in the complete whitebox cohort: Clang had 10 failed runs / 13 failed verdicts; MSVC had one failed run / two failed verdicts. Other cohorts passed all 300 repetitions. A preceding independent run also captured natural timing failures on both compilers. The captured PFX stalls explain deadlines crossed in the complete cohort; the two original positive tests have longer deadlines and did not naturally reproduce their original exact pair in these experiments.

The reproducible probe is retained in the diagnostic commit. On Windows with the [workflow's native build prerequisites](https://github.com/Milky2018/wasmoon/blob/ecc611eba875b53f852d33692f53be835701dd2a/.github/workflows/check.yml):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Milky2018/wasmoon.git
cd wasmoon
git checkout ecc611eba875b53f852d33692f53be835701dd2a
moon update
python scripts/diagnose_http_timing.py --output target/http-timing --repeats 300
```

The script temporarily instruments the installed dependency and the downstream test boundaries, then restores their original bytes. Its JSON summaries and per-run verdicts are diagnostic observations, not clean-source acceptance receipts. It also runs a separately labelled **deliberate 3500ms synchronous stall control**: that reproduces the original outer 3s timeout plus empty-body failure while the TLS test itself passes. The artificial delay is not presented as measured natural PFX latency.

The original uninstrumented CI failure had no API timeline, so we cannot establish its specific blocking call retrospectively. The shorter natural PFX stalls and cross-task interference above are directly recorded.

## Expected behavior / possible boundary

Potentially blocking credential preparation should not monopolize the coroutine/event-loop thread. A blocking Job/Worker boundary could prepare owned credentials while the requesting coroutine suspends, then deliver completion with explicit ownership, error and cancellation cleanup. Reusing prepared credentials may also reduce repeated setup, but caching alone would not address a slow first import or cache miss.

Downstream we are isolating the TLS fixture from HTTP timing assertions, retaining their deadlines and verification expectations. This avoids cross-test contamination; it does not repair the blocking async-library path described here.


## Downstream isolation regression

The downstream mitigation is committed as [c5aa9c36](https://github.com/Milky2018/wasmoon/commit/c5aa9c36965ae48675227a79ed158711cf426ef1): the TLS trust test now exercises public APIs in a separate blackbox executable. HTTP deadline tests remain in the whitebox executable. No async dependency code or HTTP deadlines were changed.

A permanent test-only mode deliberately blocks the first TLS setup for 3200ms. Temporarily putting the same test back into the shared whitebox executable reproduces the original outer TimeoutError and empty-body failures while the TLS test passes. The isolated layout passes all 32 HTTP tests in both parallel and serialized executable modes with the same control enabled. [Local source hashes, counterfactual and receipts](https://github.com/Milky2018/wasmoon/blob/c5aa9c36965ae48675227a79ed158711cf426ef1/docs/evidence/portable-interpreter-2026-10-19/tls-isolation-local.json) explicitly retain their dirty precommit macOS provenance; Windows CI for this downstream change is pending. This mitigation does not remove the synchronous PFX import from async itself.

title: Expose a transport-independent TLS session API
body:
The public TLS API currently couples TLS progress to an asynchronous `Reader`/`Writer`: the client/server constructors perform the handshake, and reads, writes, and shutdown drive the underlying transport. `client_from_pair` and `server_from_pair` allow custom transports, but still leave progress and I/O driving to `Tls`.

Could the package also expose a transport-independent TLS session API, reusing its existing OpenSSL and Schannel backends?

This would support applications that already own their event loop or receive encrypted bytes through callbacks, and need to advance TLS without giving the TLS layer ownership of transport I/O or scheduling.

The useful boundary would let the caller:

- Supply received ciphertext, including fragmented input, and explicitly report transport EOF.
- Drain generated ciphertext with bounded output capacity and backpressure.
- Advance the handshake and exchange plaintext, with explicit progress states such as needing more input, needing output to be drained, handshake completion, and connection closure.
- Drive graceful TLS shutdown and retain the existing certificate-verification, hostname/SNI, trust-root, and peer-certificate capabilities.

Consumed/produced byte counts and buffer ownership should be explicit, so callers can handle partial progress without retaining borrowed buffers across calls. The existing high-level `Tls` API could remain the convenient transport adapter over the same implementation; no second TLS backend would be needed.

A useful validation would connect client and server sessions entirely through bounded in-memory byte queues, covering fragmented handshakes, partial plaintext I/O, certificate failures, EOF, and shutdown on both native backends.

Current public interface: [src/tls/pkg.generated.mbti](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/97d7672bcb43d9cc89429e458494d2de0e8622b9/src/tls/pkg.generated.mbti).

title: [js_async] ReadableStream failures cause unhandled errors with async 0.22.4
body:
## Summary

A failed browser response stream can escape as an unhandled error even when the application handles its HTTP read failure and attempts recovery. This was reproduced in SeekMoon with the installed `moonbitlang/async@0.22.4` package on the JS target, using Google Chrome and a local mock SSE response. No real model or authentication service is needed.

The application subsequently loads its conversation history successfully, but global `unhandledrejection` / `pageerror` handlers have already replaced the UI with an error page.

## Reproduction

1. Read an SSE response with `@http.Client` and `Client::read_until("\n")`, catching read errors in the application and closing the client during cleanup.
2. Have the browser response body enqueue a complete SSE event and then fail its `ReadableStream` using `controller.error(new Error("Fixture stream disconnected"))`. The failure is gated so the first event is consumed before disconnecting.
3. Observe browser `unhandledrejection` and `pageerror` events while the application performs its normal recovery GET.

The deterministic browser regression produced this sequence (identifiers omitted):

```text
POST conversation/messages 200
unhandledrejection: Fixture stream disconnected
pageerror: Fixture stream disconnected
unhandledrejection: Fixture stream disconnected
pageerror: Fixture stream disconnected
GET conversation/messages 200
```

The successful history GET demonstrates that recovery runs; the global errors nevertheless destroy the chat UI. The first-fragment display and ordinary successful-stream tests pass.

## Source evidence in the installed 0.22.4 package

In `src/js_async/readable_stream.mbt`, `ReadableStream::from_js` reads in a separate coroutine without catching the reader failure or propagating it through the public reader:

```moonbit
let worker = @coroutine.spawn(() => {
  defer w.close()
  while reader.read() is Some(chunk) {
    w.write(chunk)
  }
})
```

Also, `ReadableStream::close` releases the reader lock and calls `JsReadableStream::cancel`, whose JS binding discards the promise:

```moonbit
extern "js" fn JsReadableStream::cancel(stream : Self) -> Unit =
  #| (stream) => stream.cancel()
```

Cancellation of an already errored stream can reject, producing another unhandled rejection. These are two plausible escape paths consistent with the two observed global errors; the browser reproduction confirms the effect, but does not separately attribute each error to its originating path.

## Expected behavior

- Response-stream failures reach the application's reading task as catchable errors, without escaping from the background copying coroutine.
- Buffered data can be consumed before the read failure is reported, rather than treating an errored stream as clean EOF.
- Closing an errored stream handles the cancellation promise and produces no unhandled rejection.
- Regression tests cover both read failure and close-after-failure on the JS target.

## Current upstream status

While preparing this report, I checked [current main's readable_stream.mbt](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/main/src/js_async/readable_stream.mbt). It already contains a `worker_error` field, catches the worker failure, raises the stored error when the pipe reaches EOF, and handles the cancellation rejection. These changes appear to address the source paths above. I have **not** tested that implementation or verified which published artifact includes it; current main's `moon.mod` still declares version `0.22.4`.

Please confirm the release containing this fix and its JS regression coverage. This report records the reproducible behavior of the installed 0.22.4 package, rather than claiming that the same bug remains on current main.

title: Windows: relative symlink target type is checked against process cwd
body:
Windows `@fs.symlink` infers the target type from the process working directory even when a relative target refers to a directory next to the link.

The current implementation calls `GetFileAttributesW(target)` directly, then uses the resulting `is_dir` to select `SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_DIRECTORY` in `CreateSymbolicLinkW`:

https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/448ff7642f9c879174cbb809f59a51e7aa8b22f4/src/internal/event_loop/fs.c#L1622-L1633

### Reproduction scenario

Given this layout, with the process cwd set to `C:\work`:

```text
C:\work\
  project\
    data\             (existing directory)
    links\
```

Call:

```moonbit
@fs.symlink("project\\links\\alias", target="..\\data", force_symlink=true)
```

The relative link target refers to `C:\work\project\data`, but the attribute probe checks `C:\data`. If the latter does not exist, `is_dir` becomes false and the implementation attempts to create a file symlink for a directory target. If the process-relative location exists with a different type, it can also produce an incorrect classification. The default `force_symlink=false` path has the same issue: relative targets are ineligible for junction creation and fall back to `CreateSymbolicLinkW`.

### Expected behavior

For ordinary relative targets, determine the target type relative to the directory containing the link, while keeping the original relative target text for `CreateSymbolicLinkW`. Absolute targets and the existing junction-selection rules should retain their behavior. Windows drive-relative paths such as `C:foo` require separate consideration.

Microsoft documents the directory/file flags here:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-createsymboliclinkw

### Verification and context

This is based on inspecting current upstream main (`448ff7642f9c879174cbb809f59a51e7aa8b22f4`); I have not run this reproduction on Windows. A Windows regression test should cover a link inside a subdirectory whose relative target is an existing directory, with a process cwd that differs from the link's parent.

Found while reviewing the Moonrun cwd changes in https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/pull/2292. The upstream native implementation has the same issue independently of Moonrun's per-run cwd feature.

title: Feature request: Unix domain socket support in @socket (for local IPC)
body:
### The need

`@socket` currently provides TCP and UDP, but no Unix domain socket (AF_UNIX). We'd like an API-level counterpart for **local inter-process communication on the same host** (daemon control channels, local service discovery, D-Bus-style buses, etc.).

### Desired API shape

Ideally it would mirror the existing TCP/UDP interfaces in `@socket`:

- **Server side**: listen on a path, accept connections, and get a duplex stream connection;
- **Client side**: connect to a path and get the same connection abstraction;
- The connection should fit naturally into the `@async` task model (interoperable with `@io.Reader` / `@io.Writer`);
- **Cross-platform behavior modeled after Node**: a single `listen(path)` / `connect(path)` API — AF_UNIX paths on Unix, automatically mapped to named pipes (`\\.\\pipe\\name`) on Windows — so callers don't face two divergent APIs depending on the platform.

Exact type naming and signatures (e.g. dedicated `UnixServer`/`UnixClient`, or variants reusing the existing `TcpServer`/`Tcp` abstractions) should follow the overall decisions of this API review.

### Motivation

Our toolchain has a management channel between a CLI and a resident DNS daemon: the CLI performs singleton detection, status queries, and hot updates of configuration and records. The Node implementation is built on `net.Server` + a unix socket and works well; after migrating to MoonBit, the lack of a corresponding capability forced us to hand-wrap C FFI just to keep the protocol compatible. This is currently the only hard blocker on our migration path. Other ecosystem projects (e.g. a D-Bus client, a local-IPC library) have similarly had to hand-roll or work around the same gap, so this doesn't look like an isolated need.

### References

Node (`net`), Go, and Python's standard library all treat local sockets as first-class citizens, and Node's path→named-pipe mapping demonstrates that a single API can cover both platforms. Since `moonbitlang/async` is planned to be merged into `moonbitlang/core` (#583), we hope this can be added to the review checklist before the API surface is finalized, so the standard library surface doesn't ship with this gap.

title: Support opt-in process groups and descendant cleanup for managed processes
body:
Stopping a command launched with `@process.spawn` can leave ordinary descendants running. Please consider opt-in process-group ownership at spawn time, with cancellation semantics that finish group cleanup before returning.

## Reproduction and impact

On macOS, using async 0.22.4:

1. Spawn `sh -c 'sleep 30 & echo $!; wait'` with `cancel_handler=@process.hard_cancel()` and capture the printed descendant PID.
2. Cancel the process and await its completion (handling cancellation).
3. `kill -0 <descendant-pid>` still succeeds. Clean up the probe with `kill -KILL <descendant-pid>`.

We reproduced this twice through SeekMoon's `ShellExecution.stop()`. An earlier reproduction also used a TCP listener: stopping the wrapper reported success while the listener remained alive and kept its port occupied. The child did not daemonize or create a new session. Direct execution of the listener stopped correctly.

Downstream reproduction and investigation: https://github.com/moonbitlang/openseek/issues/1832

## Current limitation

The same relevant implementation remains on main at `00aa493c5a674988dc0f4dc3f9bf0a0e654427ac` (source inspection, not a fresh runtime test of that revision):

- [Unix cancellation](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/00aa493c5a674988dc0f4dc3f9bf0a0e654427ac/src/process/unix.c#L144-L150) signals the direct PID.
- [POSIX spawning](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/00aa493c5a674988dc0f4dc3f9bf0a0e654427ac/src/internal/event_loop/thread_pool.c#L1468-L1477) does not establish an isolated process group.
- [Cancellation handling](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/00aa493c5a674988dc0f4dc3f9bf0a0e654427ac/src/process/process.mbt#L242-L250) runs the cancellation handler as a background task while waiting for the direct child. A TERM/wait/KILL handler can therefore be cancelled when that child exits, before it finishes cleaning up surviving descendants.

Changing SIGKILL to SIGTERM alone does not establish descendant ownership. Killing the inherited process group is unsafe, and setting the child's group from the parent after spawn races with exec.

## Requested capability

- Opt-in isolated process-group creation for managed `spawn`/`run`, established during launch; preserve existing defaults.
- A way to signal the owned group, including after its original leader exits.
- Cleanup completion independent of the direct child's lifetime, so a grace period and escalation cannot silently stop halfway through. Reporting that the direct child was reaped should remain distinct from confirming descendant cleanup.
- Document the boundary: descendants that deliberately leave the group can escape. On Windows, equivalent ownership would normally need a Job Object; a new process group alone is insufficient.

Native POSIX support would already let SeekMoon isolate its outer `moon`/`moonrun` job; ordinary processes launched inside Wasm would inherit that group. Exposing the capability to callers compiled to Wasm would additionally require matching moonrun host imports. This request does not assume the Wasm ABI must change for the downstream Native fix.

Related: #643 requests session isolation for `spawn_orphan` so a process can survive terminal closure. This issue concerns cancellation and cleanup of managed commands; the spawn-time isolation machinery may be shared.

title: Windows: fs.rename follows junctions and renames the target directory
body:
`@fs.rename` on Windows follows an NTFS junction and renames its target directory instead of renaming the junction itself.

Reproduced with `moonbitlang/async@0.22.4`, native Windows, and `moon 0.1.20260920 (914d7da 2026-09-20)`. The same handle-opening flags are present in current `main` at commit `00aa493c5a674988dc0f4dc3f9bf0a0e654427ac` (source inspected; runtime reproduction used 0.22.4).

## Reproduction

In a native MoonBit package depending on `moonbitlang/async@0.22.4`, import:

```moonbit
import {
  "moonbitlang/async",
  "moonbitlang/async/fs",
}
```

Save the following as `rename_test.mbt`, then run `moon test --target native`:

```moonbit
async test "rename a Windows junction" {
  let root = @fs.tmpdir(prefix="async-rename-repro-")
  defer @fs.rmdir(root, recursive=true)
  let target = root + "/target"
  let link = root + "/link"
  let renamed = root + "/renamed-link"
  @fs.mkdir(target)
  @fs.write_file(target + "/payload.txt", b"payload")
  // On Windows this creates a junction for the existing local directory.
  @fs.symlink(target~, link)
  @fs.rename(link, renamed, replace=false)
  println("original target exists: \{@fs.exists(target)}")
  println("original link is still a link: \{@fs.kind(link, follow_symlink=false) is SymLink}")
  println("renamed entry is a link: \{@fs.kind(renamed, follow_symlink=false) is SymLink}")
  println("payload moved to renamed entry: \{@fs.exists(renamed + "/payload.txt")}")
}
```

The reproduction operates only inside a newly created temporary directory.

## Actual behavior

The rename succeeds, but prints:

```text
original target exists: false
original link is still a link: true
renamed entry is a link: false
payload moved to renamed entry: true
```

The real target directory is now at `renamed-link`, while `link` is left dangling.

## Expected behavior

`target` and its contents should remain at their original location. The junction itself should move from `link` to `renamed-link`, retaining its target.

This matters for file managers: a user renaming or moving a link can unintentionally move the actual target directory. A later deletion of the renamed entry would then delete that directory rather than just a link.

## Likely cause

In [`moonbitlang_async_rename_sync`](https://github.com/moonbitlang/async/blob/00aa493c5a674988dc0f4dc3f9bf0a0e654427ac/src/internal/event_loop/fs.c), the Windows branch opens `old_path` with:

```c
FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL | FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS
```

It omits `FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT`, so `CreateFileW` follows the junction before `SetFileInformationByHandle` renames the opened object. Opening the reparse point itself should preserve link-rename semantics.

The runtime reproduction above covers an NTFS directory junction. File/directory symbolic links and dangling links would also be useful upstream regression cases; they were not runtime-tested in this report.

title: async fn main is not recognized as the entry point unless an async subpackage is imported
body:
## Summary

`async fn main` is only recognized as the program entry point when the package also imports **at least one `moonbitlang/async` subpackage** (e.g. `moonbitlang/async/process`). Importing only the main package `moonbitlang/async` is not enough — `moon build` treats the package as a library and `moon run` fails with:

```text
Error: `src/a` is not a main package
```

## Reproduction

Single module, two executable packages side by side (moon.work workspace).

`moon.mod`:

```toml
name = "probe/ap"

version = "0.0.1"

source = "src"

import {
  "moonbitlang/async@0.22.4",
}
```

`src/a/moon.pkg` — imports **only the main package**:

```moonbit
import {
  "moonbitlang/async",
}

pkgtype(kind: "executable")
```

`src/a/main.mbt`:

```moonbit
async fn main {
  println("A-RAN")
}
```

`src/b/moon.pkg` — identical, but also imports `moonbitlang/async/process`:

```moonbit
import {
  "moonbitlang/async",
  "moonbitlang/async/process",
}

pkgtype(kind: "executable")
```

`src/b/main.mbt`:

```moonbit
async fn main {
  println("B-RAN")
}
```

## Observed

```text
$ moon run src/a --target native
Error: `src/a` is not a main package

$ moon run src/b --target native
B-RAN
```

Controlled bisect inside one module: identical `async fn main`, flipping only the subpackage import flips recognition. Verified with multiple runs per variant.

## Expected

Per the README quick start, importing `moonbitlang/async` should be sufficient for `async fn main` to be recognized. If linking the runtime entry requires a subpackage by design, the build should at least emit a clear diagnostic instead of silently skipping the entry.

## Notes

- All official examples (`cat`, `tcp_ping_pong`, `http_file_server`, …) import at least one async subpackage (`async/process`, `async/socket`, …), which is why they don't hit this — easy to miss.
- Happy to bisect further if the trigger is something else inside the subpackage (patch registration vs. event-loop linkage).

## Environment

- moon 0.1.20260920 (914d7da) / moonc 0.10.14
- target: native, Debian 12 (WSL2, x86_64)
- moonbitlang/async@0.22.4

title: spawn_orphan: add an opt-in way to start the child in a new session (like Node's detached / Python's start_new_session)
body:
## Summary

Feature request, plus a documentation clarification.

`@process.spawn_orphan` is documented as being for a process that should "keep running after parent process terminates". On Unix it does, as long as the controlling terminal stays open. But the child remains in the caller's session and process group, so when the terminal closes it receives `SIGHUP` and exits. It also starts with every signal reset to its default, so `SIGHUP` terminates it.

That is standard Unix behaviour: `cmd &` in a shell behaves the same way. Other process libraries make detaching opt-in:
- Node: `spawn(…, { detached: true })`
- Python: `subprocess.Popen(…, start_new_session=True)`

Today `spawn_orphan` has no equivalent, so a program that wants a child to survive its terminal has to start it through `nohup` or `setsid`. `nohup` isn't available on every platform, and `setsid` isn't a standard command on macOS.

## Request

1. **An opt-in parameter,** e.g. `spawn_orphan(…, new_session? : Bool = false)`. On Unix it would start the child in a new session, via `POSIX_SPAWN_SETSID` where available (glibc ≥ 2.26; macOS also defines it) or `setsid()` in the child. A new process group (`POSIX_SPAWN_SETPGROUP` with pgroup `0`) would be a portable fallback, since the terminal's hangup `SIGHUP` goes only to the foreground process group and the session leader. On Windows it could do nothing, or map to `DETACHED_PROCESS`.
2. **A doc note** on `spawn_orphan`: an orphan still shares the caller's terminal session, so closing the terminal ends it unless it is started in a new session.

The current spawn code, for reference (`src/internal/event_loop/thread_pool.c`, `spawn_job_worker`, 0.22.4):

```c
posix_spawnattr_setflags(&attr, POSIX_SPAWN_SETSIGMASK | POSIX_SPAWN_SETSIGDEF);
...
sigfillset(&all_signals);
posix_spawnattr_setsigdefault(&attr, &all_signals);
```

## How we ran into it

OpenSeek starts a long-lived local web server (`moonx moonbitlang/inspect --ensure --watch`) with `spawn_orphan`, from both its TUI (`/inspect`) and `openseek run --inspect`. The server is meant to outlive the program and be shared. It worked while the program ran, but when the terminal closed the server exited (reproduced in a pty on macOS). We now start it as `nohup moonx …`, falling back to plain `moonx` where there is no `nohup`:
- https://github.com/moonbitlang/openseek/pull/1855
- https://github.com/moonbitlang/openseek_tui/pull/6

With a `new_session` option, both could drop `nohup`.

To reproduce: from a program started in a terminal, `spawn_orphan("sleep", ["600"])`, let the program exit, then close the terminal. `sleep` is gone.

title: http: support extension request methods (WebDAV PROPFIND, REPORT, custom API methods)
body:
### Problem

`RequestMethod` in `moonbitlang/async/http` is a closed enum holding exactly the nine
standard methods. `Client::request` only accepts this enum, and internally
`Sender::send_request` (src/http/send.mbt) matches on it to write the request line.
There is no public API that accepts a raw method name, so extension methods cannot be sent:

- WebDAV (RFC 4918): PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, MKCOL, COPY, MOVE, LOCK, UNLOCK
- Versioned editing (RFC 3253): REPORT, VERSION-CHECKOUT, etc.
- Custom methods used by API gateways and internal protocols

The server side is closed the same way: `Reader::read_request` (src/http/parser.mbt)
matches the method token exhaustively and raises `BadRequest` for anything unknown,
so a `moonbitlang/async` HTTP server cannot receive WebDAV requests either.

For comparison, raw methods are the norm elsewhere: Go's `http.NewRequest(method string, ...)`,
Rust reqwest's `Method::from_bytes`, Node.js `http.request({ method })`, and axios/fetch
all accept arbitrary method names.

### Proposal (either would unblock us)

1. Add an `Other(String)` variant to `RequestMethod`:
   - client: `Sender::send_request` writes the payload verbatim as the request-line token;
     optionally validate it against the RFC 7230 `tchar` set and reject malformed tokens.
   - parser: `should_not_have_body` treats unknown methods conservatively
     (fall through to the existing status-code-based rules).
   - server: `Reader::read_request` parses unknown tokens into `Other(name)`.
   The existing `derive(Eq, Hash, ToJson)` keeps working with a payload variant.
2. Or, minimal intrusion: a raw-method entry point such as
   `Client::request_raw(method : String, path : StringView, extra_headers? : Headers) -Unit`,
   implemented by generalizing `Sender::send_request` to take the token as a string.

Happy to follow up with a PR if the direction is agreed.
